newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PNG reassures Australia over mercenaries.
newsitem.headline: PNG reassures Australia over mercenaries.

text.p: Papua New Guinea, facing international criticism over its plan to use mercenaries to end the war on Bougainville, has pledged not to send soldiers of fortune to its secessionist island.
Foreign Minister Kilroy Genia said he had assured Australia that African private soldiers brought in to train government troops would not now be used on Bougainville.
"We are a responsible government and will not in any way engage these consultants on the ground in Bougainville," Genia said in a weekend statement received in Canberra on Monday.

Genia's assurance goes back on an earlier declaration by PNG Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan that the mercenaries, who currently number around 40, might go to Bougainville as advisers, although not as combatants.
It might also remove a major source of concern for neighbours such as Australia and New Zealand, although Canberra and Wellington are opposed to any use of mercenaries.
Amid the row Australian Prime Minister John Howard and Chan held unannounced talks at Howard's official harbourside residence in Sydney on Sunday.

Howard refused to give details of the five-hour talks, but said in a radio interview on Monday the meeting had focused on Bougainville and Chan's decision to employ mercenaries to help end the nine-year rebellion.
"We had a very detailed talk and we canvassed a whole lot of things," said Howard, who sought the meeting while Chan was in Sydney visiting relatives.
"We are quite strong in our view about the mercenaries and I made that clear to him."

Genia said he had phoned Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer on Friday to assure him the mercenaries would not go to Bougainville and that Papua New Guinea remained committed to a peaceful solution to the war.

The impoverished South Pacific nation has hired British-based Sandline International at a cost of A$36 million (US$28 million) to train its inexpert and under-resourced troops and acquire sophisticated weapons.

But Canberra had expressed concern the mercenaries would be used for a surgical strike to wipe out the rebel leadership on the mountainous, jungle-clad island, 800 kilomatres (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby.
"I want to categorically deny that we have engaged Sandline International as 'mercenaries' to eliminate our own people, especially on Bougainville," Genia said.
Thousands of people, mainly civilians, have died in the rebellion from fighting, disease and a lack of medical care.
"We worry about the introduction of mercenaries into our region -- it's never happened before," Howard said.
"They don't have a very savoury track record. We think there are worries for the Papua New Guinea government if the mercenaries are there. It's a very unstable situation."
Asked about the possibility of Australian troops training Papua New Guinea's soldiers, Howard said "any reasonable alternative" was better than using mercenaries, but he would not elaborate.
